items.q: Since the new library (A) opens last spring, hundreds of students (B) have borrowed books from it (C) every week, and the number (D) is still rising.
items.explanation: After since the starting point is a finished past event, so it takes the past simple: opened last spring. The present perfect belongs in the main clause (have borrowed).

items.q: Each of the volunteers (A) who cleaned the beach last Sunday (B) were given a T-shirt (C) as a thank-you gift (D) from the local council.
items.explanation: Each is the subject and is always singular, even when followed by of the volunteers: each … was given.

items.q: After finishing secondary school, my elder brother (A) hopes to study (B) abroad and become (C) engineer like our father, (D) who builds bridges.
items.explanation: A singular countable noun naming a job needs an article: become an engineer, a doctor, a teacher.

items.q: The coach was (A) disappointed with the result, (B) yet he praised the players for (C) their effort and told them not to be (D) afraid from making mistakes.
items.explanation: The adjective afraid is followed by of + noun or -ing form: afraid of making mistakes.

items.q: The (A) discover of penicillin in 1928 (B) changed medicine forever, (C) although its importance (D) was not fully understood for many years.
items.explanation: After the and before of we need a noun, not a verb: the discovery of penicillin.

items.q: After saving pocket money for a year, Minh and (A) his sister finally bought (B) theirselves new bicycles (C) so that they could cycle (D) to school together.
items.explanation: The reflexive pronoun for they is themselves; theirselves does not exist in English.

items.q: Jupiter, (A) the largest planet in the solar system, (B) also spins (C) more faster than any other planet, completing one turn (D) in under ten hours.
items.explanation: A one-syllable adjective or adverb forms its comparative with -er alone; more and -er are never used together: spins faster than.

items.q: Our teacher says that many students (A) would score higher marks (B) in the listening test (C) if they (D) will practise with English films at home.
items.explanation: Would in the main clause signals a second conditional, so the if-clause takes the past simple: if they practised. Will is not used after if in an ordinary conditional (if they practise / practised, not if they will practise).

items.q: The tour guide (A) said us that the temple (B) had been built in the eleventh century (C) and that it (D) was still used by local people.
items.explanation: In reported speech tell takes a direct object (told us that …) but say does not; you would need said to us.

items.q: The old bridge (A) at the end of our street, (B) that was built by the French, (C) is going to be replaced (D) next year.
options: at the end of our street
items.explanation: The clause between commas is non-defining (extra information), and a non-defining relative clause must use which, never that.

items.q: My father (A) rarely watches television, but he (B) never misses the news, (C) so he knows always (D) what is happening in the world.
items.explanation: An adverb of frequency such as always goes before a main verb: he always knows. (It goes after be and after auxiliaries.)

items.q: During the storm last night, (A) the wind was so strong (B) that several trees fell (C) across the road and (D) made a lot of damage to cars.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is do damage (or cause damage); make damage is not English.

items.q: (A) Much students in our school (B) walk or cycle to class (C) because the streets nearby are (D) too narrow for cars.
items.explanation: Students is a plural countable noun, so it takes many; much is only used with uncountable nouns (much time, much water).

items.q: The match was cancelled (A) because of the heavy rain, (B) despite the fans had waited (C) outside the stadium (D) for more than two hours.
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form; before a full clause with a subject and verb we need the conjunction although / even though.

items.q: By the time the fire engines (A) reached the warehouse, (B) most of the building (C) has already burned down, and the workers (D) were standing in the street.
items.explanation: By the time + past simple describes an action completed before another past moment, which needs the past perfect: had already burned down.

items.q: Physics (A) is my favourite subject (B) because the experiments (C) we do in the laboratory (D) explains how the world works.
items.explanation: The subject of the verb is the plural noun experiments (not laboratory), so the verb must be plural: the experiments … explain. (Physics is a singular subject name, so is is correct.)

items.q: (A) A Mekong River flows through six countries (B) before it reaches the sea, (C) and millions of people (D) depend on it for food.
items.explanation: Names of rivers, seas and oceans take the definite article: the Mekong River, the Red River, the Pacific.

items.q: The new sports centre (A) opposite the market (B) is famous of its swimming pool, (C) which is open (D) until ten o'clock at night.
items.explanation: The adjective famous collocates with for when we say what something is known for: famous for its swimming pool.

items.q: Doctors say that children (A) who sleep fewer than eight hours (B) a night often find it (C) difficultly to concentrate (D) in lessons the next day.
items.explanation: In the pattern find it + adjective + to-infinitive, the word describing it must be an adjective: find it difficult to concentrate.

items.q: The two brothers (A) started a small repair shop (B) in their garage, (C) and within a year (D) it customers came from all over the district.
items.explanation: Before a noun we need the possessive determiner its (the shop's customers), not the subject pronoun it.

items.q: Travelling by train is (A) more cheap than flying, (B) and it also gives you (C) a much better view (D) of the countryside.
items.explanation: Short adjectives like cheap form the comparative with -er: cheaper than. More is used with longer adjectives (more expensive).

items.q: If people (A) recycled more of their rubbish, (B) there will be far less plastic (C) floating in the rivers (D) and oceans.
items.explanation: The past simple in the if-clause (recycled) makes this a second conditional, so the result clause needs would, not will.

items.q: When the headmaster (A) came into the classroom, he asked (B) the monitor (C) why was the board still dirty (D) after the break.
options: why was the board still dirty
items.correction: why the board was still dirty
items.explanation: A reported question uses statement word order (subject before verb) and no question inversion: asked why the board was still dirty.

items.q: Marie Curie, (A) whose research on radioactivity (B) won her two Nobel Prizes, (C) was born in Warsaw, a city (D) where she left at the age of twenty-four.
items.explanation: Where replaces a place adverbial (in/at a place), but here the city is the object of left (she left the city), so the relative pronoun must be which or that.

items.q: Excuse me, could you tell me (A) where is the post office, (B) because I have to send (C) this parcel to my aunt (D) before it closes?
items.explanation: After Could you tell me the question becomes an indirect question, so the subject comes before the verb: where the post office is.

items.q: My sister (A) has decided to (B) make a course in graphic design (C) next year so that she can (D) work for an advertising company.
items.explanation: We take (or do) a course; make a course is not a natural English collocation.

items.q: Farmers in the delta say that (A) this year's harvest is poor (B) because there has been (C) too few rain since March (D) and the soil is dry.
items.explanation: Rain is uncountable, so it takes little; few is only used with plural countable nouns (too few showers).

items.q: The road was closed (A) after the landslide, (B) so the villagers (C) had to walk to the market (D) unless the bridge was repaired.
options: had to walk to the market
items.explanation: Unless means if … not and gives a condition, which makes no sense here; the walking continued up to the moment of repair, so the time conjunction until is needed.

items.q: While my mother (A) was cooking dinner last night, (B) the lights were suddenly going out, (C) and we had to (D) finish the meal by candlelight.
options: the lights were suddenly going out
items.explanation: The longer background action takes the past continuous (was cooking), but the short, sudden event that interrupts it takes the past simple: the lights went out.

items.q: Students (A) must to hand in their science projects (B) by Friday, or the teacher (C) will not accept them, (D) however good they are.
items.explanation: A modal verb such as must is followed by the bare infinitive, never to: must hand in. (Compare have to hand in, which does take to.)
